policy.publicRepository: Store bibliographic metadata, claim summaries, short necessary quotations, stable locators and asset provenance only.
policy.privateResearch: Copyrighted books, extracted text and research-only media remain in PaperLibrary or the standalone research archive.
policy.generatedReferences: Generated images may interpret registered sources but never become evidence for a historical or engineering claim.
policy.rights: Research utility and permission to ship are separate decisions. Every shipped asset requires an item-level rights record.

sources.citation: Neil A. Armstrong interview in Curtis Peebles, ed., The Spoken Word II: Recollections of Dryden History, Beyond the Sky, NASA SP-2011-4542, Monographs in Aerospace History 42.

supports: Armstrong denied that antiaircraft fire directly caused the damage and recalled striking an antiaircraft cable.
He estimated that six to eight feet of the right wing was removed.
He estimated an altitude near 500 feet while cautioning that he did not remember it exactly.
He identified Major John Carpenter as the flight lead and USAF exchange officer.
He recalled that they rejected landing because slowing could produce an uncontrollable snap.
He recalled flying south, ejecting near Pohang/K-3 and being recovered by Goodell Warren in a jeep.

limits: The interview was recorded approximately fifty years after the incident.
The interviewer supplies 3 September 1951; Armstrong does not independently state the date in this exchange.
The transcript records a retrospective explanation, not the words spoken over the radio during the sortie.

sources.citation: Samuel J. Cox, H-Gram 033, Naval History and Heritage Command, 2019.

supports: VF-51 service from USS Essex, armed reconnaissance west of Wonsan, BuNo 125122, cable damage, wing loss, ejection and recovery in friendly territory.
The contemporary report attributed the incident to antiaircraft fire and a pole, while Armstrong later attributed it to a cable.

limits: The source uses 5 September 1951 while other official archival metadata and Armstrong's logbook as reproduced by Hansen use 3 September.
The source alternates between F9F-2 and F9F-3 descriptions.

sources.citation: NHHC catalog L38-02.07.013, Ensign Neil Armstrong, F9F Pilot, Korean War Recon Mission, Wonsan.

supports: A contemporary visual reference for Armstrong as an ensign.
The catalog associates the image with a 3 September 1951 reconnaissance mission against transportation and storage facilities south of Majon-ni, west of Wonsan.

limits: The caption's phrase shot down does not resolve the mechanism of damage.
The catalog record alone does not establish the complete sortie sequence.

sources.citation: USS Essex Korean Combat Action Report, 18 August-21 September 1951, NHHC Post-1946 Reports collection AR/59.
limits: The report is identified but page-level acquisition and review remain pending.
A contemporary report may preserve an initial operational account that Armstrong later corrected.

sources.citation: James R. Hansen, First Man: The Life of Neil A. Armstrong, Simon & Schuster trade paperback, 2012; first published 2005. ISBN 978-1-4767-2781-3.

supports: A detailed synthesis of the mission, the competing contemporary account, the cable interpretation, wing damage, Carpenter inspection, ejection near K-3 and ground recovery.
The reproduced logbook entry supports 3 September 1951.

limits: Copyrighted secondary source; no book pages or extracted text may enter the public repository.
Use it to locate and compare primary records rather than as a radio transcript.

sources.citation: Warren Thompson, F9F Panther Units of the Korean War, Osprey Combat Aircraft 103, 2014.

supports: VF-51, USS Essex, BuNo 125122, F9F-2 identification, armed-reconnaissance target area, approximate attack speed and broad ejection sequence.

limits: The narrative repeats the earlier antiaircraft-fire and telegraph-pole account that conflicts with Armstrong's own later explanation.
Copyrighted source; image plates and text remain research-only.

sources.citation: James A. Field Jr., History of United States Naval Operations: Korea, U.S. Government Printing Office, 1962.
limits: Useful for operational context; incident-specific locators have not yet been identified.
